title: Sumaila and the Question at the Back

pages.text: During Mathematics, Madam Adwubi taught a new lesson on halves. Sitting at the back of the classroom, Sumaila did not understand what “half” meant. Everyone around him was nodding, so he nodded quietly too.
sentences: During Mathematics, Madam Adwubi taught a new lesson on halves.
Sitting at the back of the classroom, Sumaila did not understand what “half” meant.
Everyone around him was nodding, so he nodded quietly too.
pages.alt: At a wooden desk at the back of a bright Ghanaian classroom, Sumaila nods hesitantly with a puzzled brow while classmates ahead look toward Madam Adwubi.

pages.text: Sumaila wanted to ask a question, yet his heart pounded. “What if people laugh?” he worried. “What if they think I am slow?” So he stayed silent. When the bell rang, he still did not know what a half was.
sentences: Sumaila wanted to ask a question, yet his heart pounded.
“What if people laugh?” he worried.
“What if they think I am slow?” So he stayed silent.
When the bell rang, he still did not know what a half was.
pages.alt: Sumaila sitting quietly at his back desk staring down at his plain open exercise book with a worried expression as classmates pack their bags.

pages.text: The next morning, Madam Adwubi gave a short practice exercise. Sumaila stared at the first question and felt his ears grow warm. Taking a slow, steady breath, he raised his hand high. “Madam, please, I still do not understand halves,” he said.
sentences: The next morning, Madam Adwubi gave a short practice exercise.
Sumaila stared at the first question and felt his ears grow warm.
Taking a slow, steady breath, he raised his hand high.
“Madam, please, I still do not understand halves,” he said.
pages.alt: At his desk in the classroom, Sumaila takes a brave breath and raises one hand high while Madam Adwubi turns toward him kindly.

pages.text: Madam Adwubi did not laugh; she smiled warmly. “Thank you for asking, Sumaila,” she said. She drew eight red apples on the board and grouped them into two equal sets of four. “Half of eight is four. Whenever we share equally into two parts, each part is one half.”
sentences: Madam Adwubi did not laugh; she smiled warmly.
“Thank you for asking, Sumaila,” she said.
She drew eight red apples on the board and grouped them into two equal sets of four.
“Half of eight is four.
Whenever we share equally into two parts, each part is one half.”
pages.alt: Madam Adwubi smiling at the chalkboard as she points to a neat picture-only chalk drawing of eight red apples divided into two equal groups of four.

pages.text: “Oh! I was confused about that too!” whispered a girl at the next desk. Two more classmates nodded eagerly in relief. Sumaila blinked in surprise—many pupils had wondered the exact same thing, and his brave question had helped them all.

pages.alt: Several relieved classmates around Sumaila smiling and raising their hands in agreement as Sumaila beams with surprise and relief.

pages.text: At break time, Sumaila shared eight roasted groundnuts equally with his friend—four for his friend and four for himself—and understood completely. “Asking questions is how we learn,” Madam Adwubi reminded the class. “One honest question helps everyone.”

activities.question: Why did Sumaila keep quiet on the first day?
options: He worried classmates might laugh at him

activities.question: What surprised Sumaila right after Madam Adwubi explained halves?
options: Other classmates had the exact same question

activities.prompt: How do you feel when a teacher welcomes your honest question warmly?

glossary.definition: Two equal parts that make up one whole.
Something we ask when we want to learn or understand clearly.
Shared so every group receives the exact same amount.
